]]> HARRISBURG — Attorney General Dave Sunday, along with law enforcement partners, announced felony drug-dealing charges regarding over-the-counter sales of illegal THC/marijuana products in northcentral Pennsylvania.

Majid Syed, 45, owner of two Fuel On gas station/convenience stores in Cameron and Elk counties is charged with felony corrupt organizations, possession with intent to deliver, and dealing in proceeds of illegal activity.

Two employees of the Elk County store — Adnan Pillay, 33, and Haji Afzal, 64 — are charged with the same crimes regarding that Ridgway business.

All three defendants surrendered for arraignments Friday morning. Bail was set at $100,000 unsecured for Syed, and $50,000 unsecured apiece for Pillay and Afzal.

According to a collaborative, long-term investigation, the defendants knowingly sold the illegal products, which were pure marijuana or contained illegal levels of THC.

“Residents recognized these stores as scourges on their communities and called on law enforcement to act — we did, and these are the results,” Attorney General Sunday said. “These illegal products, which included packaging designed to attract children, were sold every day out of these two store fronts. As of today, that illegal activity is over.”

Earlier this year, Attorney General Sunday joined law enforcement partners in Westmoreland County to announce charges and statewide seizures of illegal THC/marijuana products, and an ongoing campaign to target “smoke shops” knowingly selling the addictive, harmful products.

Regarding the recent investigation and charges, the Office of Attorney General’s Bureau of Narcotics Investigation was assisted by the North Central Drug Task Force, Emporium Borough Police Department, Ridgway Borough Police Department, Pennsylvania State Police, and the Cameron County District Attorney’s Office and the Elk County District Attorney’s Office. 

Investigators seized numerous products from the stores and more than $10,000 cash.

The respective district attorneys’ offices will prosecute the cases. Criminal charges, and any discussion thereof, are merely allegations and all defendants are presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty.

]]> Office of Attorney General teaming with business partners on STOP sign awareness campaign at Pa. ATMs 

HARRISBURG — During National Cryptocurrency Month this October, Attorney General Dave Sunday is warning Pennsylvanians about scammers who use threats of arrest, phony investment opportunities, and online romance prospects to convince consumers to send money via cryptocurrency. 

Attorney General Sunday announced a STOP sign awareness campaign during a community event in East Stroudsburg alongside Sen. Rosemary Brown (R-40), who attended in support of efforts to protect consumers from cryptocurrency-related fraud.

The STOP sign campaign will place warning signage at cryptocurrency and Bitcoin ATMs across the Commonwealth to help interrupt scams before transactions occur. The Office of Attorney General is strongly encouraging businesses that offer these machines to prominently display the signs, reminding consumers to stop before following instructions from unexpected callers, scanning QR codes or sending money under pressure.

The signage is available for download here and here. 

Although cryptocurrency kiosks are located throughout the Commonwealth, many Pennsylvanians, especially older residents, may not be familiar with them — and why scammers prefer them as a method of payment.

Last year, the Office of Attorney General’s Bureau of Consumer Protection received about 290 scam complaints involving cryptocurrency. Most commonly, the scams involved investment or romance opportunities, and some employed threats and other scare tactics.

“Although the means of payment are different, the lures for these scams are the same. We really want to spread the word and warnings about solicitations involving cryptocurrency,” Attorney General Sunday said. “Criminals rely on fear and pressure to get victims to act before asking questions. If you receive an unexpected ask or directive to make a cryptocurrency transfer or deposit, stop and cease that communication. If you believe you have been targeted, contact my office. We are here to help.”

“In this ever-changing world, protecting our residents from scams and fraud is extremely important,” Sen. Brown said. “I sincerely appreciate Attorney General Sunday’s dedication to this important work and his continued efforts to keep Pennsylvanians informed and protected. His commitment to identifying emerging scams and bringing awareness to both the Legislature and the public helps empower our communities with the knowledge they need to recognize these threats and protect themselves and their loved ones.”

Cryptocurrency is a form of digital currency that can be purchased online or at kiosks, sometimes called Bitcoin ATMs. Scammers direct consumers to these machines to convert cash into cryptocurrency and send it to a wallet controlled by the scammer.

These transactions happen quickly and are often not traceable as a traditional bank withdrawal or transfer may be, making it very difficult for investigators to retrieve the victim’s losses.

“Cryptocurrency is the latest front in the longstanding battle against consumer fraud,” Alex Baloga, President and CEO of Pennsylvania Food Merchant Association (PFMA), said. “PFMA remains committed to protecting our members from fraud and the public, our members’ customers, from abuse. We value our partnership with OAG and law enforcement across Pennsylvania to raise awareness about crypto fraud schemes and equip the retail community to fight back against this novel threat.”

Attorney General Sunday’s Bureau of Consumer Protection has seen an uptick this year in government imposter scams involving callers who pose as representatives of county sheriff’s offices. Those scams often include a threat of arrest, and demand deposits into a Bitcoin ATM using a QR code provided by the scammer.

No legitimate law enforcement agency or court will direct you to a cryptocurrency kiosk to pay a fine, resolve a warrant, or avoid arrest.

  • In one instance, a Pennsylvanian received a (fraudulent) call that appeared to come from a local police department regarding an outstanding warrant. The target was ordered to purchase $4,000 in cryptocurrency through a kiosk, which they did. That currency was sent to a scammer. Our office was able to retrieve back some of that money.
  • Other scams begin with a relationship developed over social media or a messaging app. In one case, a consumer reported sending $81,000 through wire transfers for purported cryptocurrency investments after developing a romantic relationship with someone on WhatsApp. The scammer said the investments were for their future together. The consumer realized it was a scam when he could not withdraw the money without paying more.

“These scams are heartbreaking stories as they often involve a victim who is scared or thinks they have a sound investment opportunity — only to then discover their hard-earned dollars went to a scammer,” Attorney General Sunday said. “And it is so challenging to claw back the money after it is sent, that is why education and awareness are essential.”

Attorney General Sunday offers the following tips to help Pennsylvanians protect themselves:

  • Do not act on demands to use a cryptocurrency kiosk. Police, courts, banks, and legitimate technical support representatives will not instruct you to deposit cash into a crypto kiosk to resolve an emergency or protect your money.
  • Verify unexpected calls and messages independently. Caller ID can be manipulated to display a legitimate phone number. Hang up and contact the agency or business using a number from its official website. If the caller claims to be someone you know but you are suspicious, call that person back on a number you know they use.
  • Be cautious when an online relationship turns to investing. Someone you have never met who offers to teach you about cryptocurrency or pressures you to invest may be trying to steal your money.
  • Watch for promises of guaranteed profits and demands for additional payments. Fraudulent platforms may display fake earnings, then block withdrawals or demand supposed taxes or fees before releasing funds.
  • Protect your accounts. Use two-factor authentication and never share passwords, private keys, or recovery phrases that provide access to your cryptocurrency wallet.
  • Research before sending money. Independently review the company or platform and understand its transaction and conversion fees. Do not rely solely on links, testimonials, or instructions provided by someone encouraging you to invest.

Consumers who believe they have been targeted should stop sending money and report the incident promptly. Keep messages, transaction receipts, and any wallet addresses or QR codes used in the transaction.

Consumers may submit a complaint to the Office of Attorney General’s Bureau of Consumer Protection at www.attorneygeneral.gov, by emailing scams@attorneygeneral.gov, or by calling 1-800-441-2555.

]]> Pennsylvania to receive nearly $9 million in the settlement

HARRISBURG – Attorney General Dave Sunday joined a coalition of 36 attorneys general in reaching a $220 million settlement with General Motors regarding consumer data-sharing. The settlement resolves allegations that General Motors illegally sold consumers’ private driver behavior data and location information to third parties, including data brokers who then sold the data to insurance companies. For many consumers, this data was used by insurance companies in part to set insurance rates. 

Pennsylvania is expected to receive $8.67 million through the settlement. 

Additionally, the settlement requires General Motors to obtain affirmative express consent from consumers before collecting or disclosing consumer driving and location data. 

“General Motors promised consumers their personal driving data would not be shared, then turned around and essentially exploited that data by selling it to insurance providers,” Attorney General Sunday said. “This bait-and-switch tactic betrayed consumers’ trust and potentially impacted their insurance rates. Pennsylvanians deserve transparency and honesty about how their personal data is collected, shared, and used.”

From 2016 to 2024, GM enrolled millions of drivers in their Smart Driver program, which tracked their driving habits. GM pitched this tool as a way for drivers to improve their own driving safety and told drivers that they would not share their data with insurers without express consent.

However, the coalition found that GM sold this information to data brokers under contracts that specified the data was to be used for insurance products. The data brokers sold the data to insurance companies, who could then change the driver’s premium based on their driving habits. GM did not disclose to drivers that their data would be sold for this purpose.

The data GM sold was personal, identifiable, and specific. Insurers had data showing how many times a person drove their vehicle, the start and end times of each drive, how many times they braked or accelerated quickly, and whether they went faster than the speed limit. As documented in the New York Times, insurance companies then used this information to change rates, sometimes increasing their premiums. After the Times reported on these practices, GM discontinued the Smart Driver program.

The settlement also requires GM to limit the driving data it collects from consumers and protect their personal information going forward as part of a comprehensive data privacy program. The terms secured by the coalition are significantly stronger than any other resolution reached with GM for this conduct including by mandating internal and external data protection and privacy program assessments. GM also agreed to oversight and training requirements at their dealerships to protect consumers against being enrolled in data collection schemes without their consent.

The case was co-led by Washington and Oregon, assisted by the Executive Committee of Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Kentucky, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, Utah, and Vermont, and joined by the attorneys general of Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, the District Of Columbia, Florida, Hawai’i, Idaho, Kansas, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Mississippi, Nevada, New Hampshire, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota, Virginia, and Wisconsin. 

Read the settlement.

]]> HARRISBURG — Attorney General Dave Sunday announced the takedown of a Lehigh County-based “chop shop” scheme, with charges against a father and son who engaged in illegal titling and sales of stolen vehicles with counterfeit documents.

Jermaine Quinones Sr., 42, and Jermaine Quinones Jr., 18, are each charged with numerous felonies, including corrupt organizations, theft by deception, washing vehicle titles, and insurance fraud.

The older Quinones was arrested earlier this month at his Allentown home. He was arraigned on the charges and bail was set at $450,000 cash.

Jermaine Quinones Jr. was arrested Thursday. At arraignment, bail was set at $100,000.

According to a collaborative investigation between the Office of Attorney General’s Insurance Fraud Section, Pennsylvania State Police, and Monroe County Detectives, the father and son ran a chop shop throughout 2026, “washing” titles of vehicles that were known to be stolen with VINs and other information not belonging to the stolen vehicles.

Many of the vehicles were sold on Facebook Marketplace.

“This criminal conduct is harmful in many ways, as it defrauds the Commonwealth’s vehicle titling system and insurance providers, and unsuspecting buyers who are left with ‘dirty’ vehicles,” Attorney General Sunday said. “The vehicle titling and registration system exists to protect consumers and insurance providers, and ensure vehicles on Commonwealth roadways are safe.”

Many of the vehicles were new and of high value, including 2026 model Infiniti QX60 ($67,599 value), Acura Integra ($35,950), and two Ford Mustangs ($32,640 and $31,890).

Between 2025 and 2026, investigators identified sales of 12 vehicles with washed paperwork, valued at nearly $500,000.

When taking Quinones Sr into custody, investigators seized a semiautomatic rifle. He is not permitted to possess firearms due to a prior felony conviction.

The case will be prosecuted by Senior Deputy Attorney General Joseph Sembrot and Deputy Attorney General Jose Perez of the Insurance Fraud Section. Criminal charges, and any discussion thereof, are merely allegations and all defendants are presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty.

]]> HARRISBURG — Attorney General Dave Sunday and the Pennsylvania State Police announced charges against the owner of two Lancaster County spas — alleged fronts for commercial sex operations.

Lijin Chen, 38, was arrested Thursday on numerous charges, including felony counts of corrupt organizations, promoting prostitution, and dealing in proceeds of unlawful activities. Bail was set at $100,000.

According to an investigation by the Office of Attorney General’s Human Trafficking Section and the state police, Chen owned Calm Spa in Manheim and Cozy Spa in Mount Joy since 2023. She is charged with advertising online the spas for commercial sex, and investigators conducted surveillance confirming commercial sex acts happened at both locations.

“Our surveillance of these locations revealed that these purported spas were used for commercial sex dates, often arranged online,” Attorney General Sunday said. “With the filing of serious criminal charges, these businesses will no longer be scourges to the community.”

Investigators spoke with numerous individuals as they left the spas, and they admitted to receiving sex acts for “tips” — ranging between $100 and $200.

Chen transported women (sex workers) to both locations, in her own vehicle and by using ride-share services.

The investigation is ongoing.

The case will be prosecuted by the Office of Attorney General’s Human Trafficking Section. Criminal charges, and any discussion thereof, are merely allegations and all defendants are presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty.

]]> HARRISBURG — Attorney General Dave Sunday, along with Pennsylvania State Police and Dauphin County law enforcement partners, announced the takedown of a drug-trafficking ring distributing methamphetamine, fentanyl and other drugs, as well as firearms.

This week, the Office of Attorney General filed charges against five individuals, following a long-term investigation that revealed drug-dealing activities in Dauphin, Blair, Cumberland, and Clinton counties.

Charged with felony drug trafficking and related offenses are:

Marcus A. Denson, Jovar Hairston, Larry Minnifield, Alisha Massa, and Gregory Johnson.

Denson is also charged with trafficking firearms, including at least one “ghost gun.”

Massa and Johnson were arrested Wednesday. Efforts are ongoing to take the other three defendants into custody.

“This criminal network directly contributed to the distribution of poisons that ravage families and communities, and made illegal transfers of firearms that threaten the sanctity of neighborhoods,” Attorney General Sunday said. “With our partners, over time, we constructed cases against all the defendants and effectively shut down this network with very serious charges.”

During the course of the investigation, officials seized six firearms and surveilled numerous sales of fentanyl, methamphetamine, and other drugs involving the five charged.

Denson is prohibited from possessing firearms due to a prior felony conviction.

The cases will be prosecuted by the Office of Attorney General’s Drug Strike Force Section. Criminal charges, and any discussion thereof, are merely allegations and all defendants are presumed innocent until and unless proven guilty.

]]> Sentencing is scheduled for Jan. 21 in Allegheny County

HARRISBURG — Attorney General Dave Sunday announced that Patrick Vereb Sr., owner of western Pennsylvania-based Eternity Pet Memorial, pleaded guilty to all charges regarding theft of more than $650,000 from customers who paid for pet burial and cremation services between 2021 and 2024.

Vereb, 72, pleaded guilty to all charges, and will be sentenced on the lead felony — first-degree theft by deception — on Jan. 21, following a sentencing hearing.

Also Thursday, Vereb’s bail was revoked and he was committed to prison.

Vereb was charged last year with improper disposal of thousands of dogs and cats for which owners paid for cremations, burials, returns of ashes, and other services. According to the Office of Attorney General investigation, Vereb took money in exchange for private cremation services, then disposed of many of the pets at a landfill and provided customers with ashes of other, unknown animals.

More than 6,500 victims from Allegheny, Armstrong, Washington, and Westmoreland counties were identified.

“As a pet owner, I know that losing a pet is like losing a family member, and the defendant’s conduct, without a doubt, worsened that pain for these victims,” Attorney General Sunday. “No sentence can alleviate the grief and heartache that has been caused here, but our hope is this felony conviction provides a measure of closure as it involves the defendant taking responsibility and admitting to what he did.”

Due to the widespread impact, and duration of the criminal conduct, following the filing of charges, the Office of Attorney General launched a webpage to identify and make contact with as many victims as possible.

Many of those victims submitted victim impact statements which will be submitted to the court for consideration at sentencing.

Nearly a dozen veterinary practices and businesses worked with the Office of Attorney General to confirm that Vereb collected more than $650,000 in fees from pet owners who were promised a private cremation for their pet, but did not receive the actual ashes of their pet.

Eternity Pet Memorial received the pets directly from consumers or through area veterinarians.

The case is being prosecuted by Senior Deputy Attorneys General Kara Rice and Aaron McKendry.

]]> HARRISBURG – Attorney General Dave Sunday today announced a settlement with Gillece Services, LP, Gillece Plumbing and Heating, Inc., Thomas Gillece Sr., Thomas Gillece Jr., and two former Gillece technicians, resolving allegations that these defendants misled Pennsylvania consumers into paying for unnecessary home improvement work (particularly, sewer pipe replacements) and engaged in scare tactics, amongst other allegations.

The settlement, in the form of a Consent Order, consists of $700,000 in consumer restitution, $50,000 in costs, and $250,000 in suspended civil penalties. The Consent Order was filed in the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas.

“Gillece pressured consumers to undergo expensive home repair work that was oftentimes unnecessary,” Attorney General Sunday said. “Gillece advertised specials that they knew they would not honor, leaving consumers on the hook for work they did not want or need. This settlement would not have been possible without the assistance of the consumers who brought this issue to the attention of the Office of Attorney General.”

The lawsuit filed by the Office of Attorney General alleged that Gillece lured consumers experiencing sewer back-ups through the “$93 or Free Clog Crusher Special.” While the offer promised to “crush” consumers’ sewer clogs for $93 or the service would be free, once the Gillece technicians arrived at consumers’ homes, many consumers were told that their clogs could not be cleared using a snake but could only be cleared through costly excavation work. The lawsuit alleged that the excavation work was unnecessary and that the sewer lines could, in fact, have been cleared without digging up their properties. Many consumers were allegedly told that their sewer pipes had physical defects requiring replacement and later discovered that such defects did not exist.

The lawsuit also alleged that Gillece engaged in scare tactics in attempting to get consumers to sign home improvement contracts, such as telling consumers that they had gas leaks or cracked heat exchangers – diagnoses that were later discredited by third parties, including the consumers’ natural gas utility companies. The lawsuit also alleged that Gillece’s work was often shoddy and inconsistent with its written warranties and that Gillece, at times, failed to provide consumers with copies of their contracts and notices of cancellation at the time of sale, as required by law. The lawsuit contained other allegations that were ruled on in the Office’s favor on summary judgment, including that Gillece: 1) failed to permit consumers to cancel home improvement contracts within three days and penalized consumers who cancelled by entering their properties without their permission; 2) made false or misleading advertising claims and offers; and 3) made misrepresentations to consumers about their flat-rate pricing.

Under the settlement, Gillece has agreed to injunctive terms to address their allegedly deceptive practices, including, but not limited to:

  • Robust certification of Gillece’s plumbing and HVAC technicians. Specifically, any Gillece technician selling sewer excavation work or hydro jets must be certified in the Lateral Assessment Certification Program offered by the National Association of Sewer Service Companies (NASSCO).
  • Gillece must document the defects that serve as the basis of their recommendation to repair or replace sewer pipes, and those defects must arise to a certain level of severity under NASSCO’s defect standards.
  • In the event Gillece cannot open a sewer line and documents defects, Gillece must make multiple attempts to get the line opened using a snake and advise consumers of their option to seek a second opinion to confirm whether additional work is necessary to open the line.
  • Gillece’s HVAC technicians must be certified by North American Technician Excellence (NATE) and utilize only carbon monoxide detectors/meters that are calibrated by the manufacturer in accordance with the manufacturer’s recommended schedule.
  • Any diagnosis by Gillece of a gas leak must generally be confirmed by the consumer’s natural gas provider prior to Gillece selling such consumers any work to repair the leak.
  • Any diagnosis by Gillece of a cracked heat exchanger or other dangerous condition must be confirmed by two of Gillece’s NATE-certified technicians.
  • Gillece must create and maintain detailed records documenting the defects and/or conditions supporting their recommendations for certain repairs or replacements and provide the Office with such documentation upon request.

Additionally, under the terms of the Consent Order, Gillece must: 1) perform their work in a workmanlike manner, consistent with their written warranties; 2) provide all consumers with copies of their contracts and notices of cancellation at the time of signing; 3) refrain from making advertising claims they know they cannot or will not honor; and 4) include in any non-disclosure or confidentiality agreements an express exception for providing information to law enforcement.

This new injunctive relief set forth in the Consent Order is in addition to the injunctive relief obtained by the Office of Attorney General on summary judgment in August 2023, when Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas entered findings that Gillece has violated numerous Pennsylvania consumer protection laws. The injunctive relief entered on summary judgement remains in effect and requires Gillece to honor consumers’ verbal requests to cancel their home improvement contracts and cease and desist from making false or misleading advertising statements and misrepresentations about their flat-rate pricing.

The settlement also bans the two former Gillece technicians named as defendants, James F. Hackwelder and Joseph A. Nikoula, from the plumbing industry for a period of five years.

Consumers who are eligible to obtain restitution as part of this settlement will be contacted by the Office of Attorney General and do not need to take any action.

This case was litigated by Assistant Chief Deputy Attorney General Jill T. Ambrose.

A settlement agreement shall not be considered as an admission of violation of the law.

]]> HARRISBURG — Attorney General Dave Sunday announced charges against a northwestern Pennsylvania pharmacy technician for diverting nearly 90,000 prescription pills from her place of employment.

Alyssa R. McDowell, 34, is charged with several felony counts of obtaining a controlled substance by misrepresentation, theft by unlawful taking, and related misdemeanors.

McDowell surrendered Tuesday morning and was arraigned, when bail was set at $100,000 unsecured.
